https://www.arbuturian.com/culture/books.text: Trending Old City, New Tricks: Lisbon’s Endless Temptations Bao, Bargains and Rooftops: A Tale of Three Japans Table for One, please: Dating Myself in Paris Spa of the Month: Low Wood Bay, Windermere Oxford, Collected Fashion Becomes Tea at The Kensington Town House Porto Montenegro: A Life Less Taxing Zoilo The Truth Brindisa, Battersea The Best Caddie on the West Coast A Summer Miscellany By Philip Cottam on August 2, 2026 Books Whether you’re reading poolside, on a delayed train, or hiding from the heat with the curtains drawn, Philip Cottam’s summer selection has range: espionage in Cold War Berlin, small-town America unravelling, a river fighting for its life, and one extraordinary woman’s journey through revolution and war… The Predicament by William Boyd Gabriel Drax, travel writer and part-time spy at the centre of The Predicament , first appeared on the scene in Gabriel’s Moon, first published in 2024. The Predicament sees Gabriel well and truly embedded in the secret world, caught between his two employers, MI6 and the KGB, as well as the internal politics of the CIA. To make matters even more complicated he becomes involved in an intense but somewhat on-off relationship with his MI6 handler. Gabriel certainly confronts several predicaments both personal and professional. It all makes for a heady mix that William Boyd handles deftly. The main thread of the story centres on a rogue element in the CIA and the build-up to the famous Kennedy visit to Cold War Berlin in the summer of 1963 and his subsequent assassination in Dallas later that year. Gabriel’s journey to Berlin starts with a dangerous mission to violence ridden Guatemala City. What happens sets the scene for what follows in Berlin. The Berlin section of the story is cleverly plotted around the Kennedy visit. It also sees Gabriel, part-time amateur agent, starting to acquire the street-smart skills and situational awareness he really needs to survive. With The Predicament Boyd has written a worthy successor to Gabriel’s Moon . Gabriel Drax is a more firmly established character and Boyd continues to make good use of his descriptive talents in creating the different atmospheres that surround Gabriel whether at home in London and Sussex or when in Berlin and Guatemala. Given the mention of a trip to Moscow by his Russian handler, it would seem that, having successfully navigated his way through the predicaments confronting him, Gabriel’s adventures in the world of espionage are not yet over. The Predicament is out now in paperback, published by Penguin . American Rust by Philipp Meyer With the upcoming mid-term American elections and the emergence of divisions amongst both traditional Republicans and, perhaps more significantly, amongst the MAGA base of the electoral alliance that swept Trump to power for a second term it would seem a good time to read or even re-read American Rust by Philipp Meyer. Published to acclaim in 2009 it was subsequently turned into a TV crime drama in 2021. In the novel Meyer sets out to illustrate the decline of the American middle class through the impact of an accidental murder in a fictional town set in an area of Pennsylvania known for its run-down and economically depressed steel towns. The narrative is driven by a series of relationships. The most important is that between two young friends and how they handle their differing responsibilities for the killing. There is then the old relationship between the mother of one of the young men and the Police Chief investigating the murder. The result is a series of conflicts of loyalty and integrity. All takes place in a community marked by declining prosperity and the accompanying tensions that arise when both aspirations and expectations have been damaged. Meyer makes effective use of a stream of consciousness technique as the mechanism through which he narrates his story. His characters are closely observed with their behaviours well imagined and their moral conflicts well-constructed. As for his writing style it is sparse, gritty and atmospheric. When first published American Rust drew comparisons with Faulkner and Steinbeck from some reviewers. It certainly opens the door onto how the frustration and despair of once prosperous communities at being sacrificed on the altar of globalisation led to the attraction of the MAGA movement for many. American Rust is published by Scribner UK . Is a River Alive? by Robert MacFarlane Robert Macfarlane first established himself as a master of the language of landscapes and mankind’s relationship with nature when he published Mountains of the Mind in 2003. Since then, he has gone on to publish several more looking at different aspects of those two themes, of which Is a River Alive? is the most recent. Is a River Alive? takes a journey, part elegiac and part an alarm call, to dying rivers and those trying to save them, in Ecuador, India and Quebec. Like all its predecessors the book is thoughtful and intriguing and opens doors onto nature in unexpected ways. Given the increasingly angry outcry against the pollution of our rivers and streams it is certainly timely. It also includes, appropriately close to his home in Cambridge, the story of a spring that because of lack of care frequently dries up damaging the landscape it feeds. In Ecuador MacFarlane visits a river and its tributaries in the cloud forest, a rain forest in the mountains where clouds linger amongst the trees. The river is threatened by exploitation of nearby mineral deposits. Damage to the purity of the water will also damage the virgin forest, its flora and fauna. The threat is underlined by MacFarlane’s companion, a scientist who has discovered previously unknown fungi. In India MacFarlane visits the three main rivers of Chennai which have been so damaged by chemical and other pollution. Here the fight for improvement is being driven by activists through the court system. In Quebec his river odyssey is completed with a canoe trip down the wild pure waters and rapids of one of the many rivers that flow through the province. It is an adventure that stands in stark contrast to the previous two journeys. Does MacFarlane answer the question that is his title? The answer is a resounding yes. He shows how both landscape and humanity can become impoverished if the rivers that feed them become polluted and die through a combination of thoughtlessness and greed. His style is not polemical. It is subtle, elegant and thought-provoking. Above all he brings the landscapes that enthral him to life . Is a River Alice? is published by Penguin . I, Vera by Miranda Seymour Miranda Seymour has written an unputdownable biography with I, Vera . She has certainly been helped by her protagonist and the turbulent times she lived through. Born a Lithuanian Princess in 1870 Vera Ignatievna Gedroits grew up to become the first woman in the Russian Empire to become a doctor at the Imperial Court, a battlefield surgeon and a professor of medicine. She was also a writer, both medical and literary, as well as an occasional poet. All this while living openly as a lesbian, getting arrested as a student political activist, surviving the violence of the October Revolution, although she did get wounded. She also avoided the frequent Bolshevik purges that followed the revolution until 1930 despite her connections with the Imperial family. Her eventful life ended two years later when she died of cancer while still in the company of her longtime partner the Countess Maria Nirod. For all her privileged upbringing and her close connection to the Imperial family Vera was in no doubt that her commitment as a doctor was especially for those who needed her skills most. It was not a coincidence that during her first job as a qualified doctor in a hospital attached to a factory she was known as the ‘people’s doctor’. She never worried about danger and became a military surgeon during the Russo-Japanese War, the First World War and the civil war that followed the October Revolution. As for her lesbianism she had to be discreet at first, especially when attached to the Imperial Court at Tsarskoe Selo (now usually called Pushkin). Her long relationship with the Countess Maria Nirod, which began during the time Vera was recovering from her wound in 1918, was more open. This was because of the more relaxed atmosphere towards social mores in the early years of post-Imperial Russia. Miranda Seymour has produced a real page-turner while at the same time remaining true to the historical record even when it contradicts Vera herself. She did write five autobiographies. Seymour also puts Vera’s significant achievements in context, whether her contributions to medical science or just in navigating the very different social and political environments of Imperial and Revolutionary Russia. Above all the story she tells of this remarkable and praiseworthy woman makes for a life-enhancing read. I, Vera is out now published by William Collins, available from Daunt Books . Photograph: KYODO/Reuters Japan At least four people killed in Japan as typhoon Dujuan triggers heavy rain, landslides Rescuers search for missing in collapsed homes after storm causes landslides, travel chaos and power outages Agence France-Presse Tue 22 Sep 2026 00.48 EDT Last modified on Tue 22 Sep 2026 01.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Typhoon Dujuan has killed at least four people and injured 22 in Japan , while tens of thousands of houses near Tokyo remained without power after the storm swept through the region, authorities said on Tuesday. Dujuan – which brought violent winds of 144km/h (89mph) – was moving away from Japan on Tuesday morning, allowing authorities to downgrade most heavy rain and landslide warnings. But the typhoon had already caused deaths, destruction and widespread chaos, including disruption of some events at the Asian Games and forcing the early closure in Tokyo of the one of the world’s biggest video game trade fairs. ‘Forcing a reckoning’: How Asia is preparing for a ‘supersized’ El Niño Read more The city of Yokosuka in Kanagawa prefecture, near Tokyo, reported multiple landslides because of the torrential rain. Mud flowing into a home killed a woman in her 60s in Yokosuka, the public ​broadcaster NHK said. Police and firefighters said they were trying to find a couple in their 70s. View image in fullscreen Rescue workers search a house hit by a landslide triggered by typhoon Dujuan in Miura, Japan. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters Local authorities in Chiba, near Tokyo, said three people were killed in a series of landslides that hit the prefecture, according to NHK. Two people, believed to have been inside homes that collapsed, were missing. Officials said 45,000 households ​were still ​without electricity in Chiba on Tuesday morning. The storm forced Japan Airlines to cancel 135 flights and All Nippon Airways to scrap 140, and more than 1.6 million residents in and around Tokyo were urged to evacuate on Monday, according to the Fire and Disaster Management Agency. The evacuations were not mandatory. View image in fullscreen A boy cycles through a flooded street as typhoon Dujuan brings heavy rain, in Ichikawa, in Chiba prefecture. Photograph: KYODO/Reuters Although Dujuan weakened as it moved north-east, it dumped record rainfall in parts of the Tokyo area. Oshima, an island about 120km south of central Tokyo, was drenched with 832mm of rain over 48 hours, more than double its average rainfall for the whole of September, NHK reported. And rainfall in Tokyo’s Edogawa ward reached a record 282.5mm over 24 hours. Japan often sees strong typhoons in the late summer and early autumn. But scientists say human-driven climate change is intensifying the risk posed by heavy rains because a warmer atmosphere holds more water. Typhoon Dujuan is the latest extreme weather event in a ⁠year of unusually intense rain, floods and tropical ​cyclones that have hit ‌regions across ‌the globe, from east Asia to North America ‌and Europe. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2k.text: Figure caption, Major protest in Spain as millions struggle to find an affordable home By Ella Kipling Published 3 October 2026, 12:35 BST Updated 2 hours ago Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to get emergency housing legislation through parliament on Friday. About 50 planned marches are taking place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona . "There is a lot of anger in the streets," said a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union, where a demonstration has already started. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city. The measures put forward by Pedro SÃ¡nchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase. Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property. Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer. His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament. Spanish PM SÃ¡nchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87 Published 1 day ago Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina SofÃ­a, which was hosting a real estate summit. Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Image source, EPA Image caption, Tens of thousands took to the streets of Madrid to protest Image source, EPA/Shuttershock Image caption, Tensions arose between some protesters and police officers in Valencia One of the biggest demonstration is happening in the capital, Madrid. Estimates of the number of participants varied widely, with the city's Tenants' Union putting it at 500,000, while government officials put the figure at 70,000. Demonstrators have been camping in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days. One protester, David, told Spanish public broadcaster RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction." On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives". It is calling for a general strike over the housing crisis. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, An encampment has been set up for days by protesters at Puerta del Sol in Madrid Image source, EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, Madrid is expected to be the site of the largest protests this weekend The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two separate decrees. The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds". The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union. MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166. Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country. However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure. SÃ¡nchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September. The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, UrbagestiÃ³n, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued. Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage Published 23 September The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction. House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE. The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.
